'''Random band matrices''' are [[Random matrix|random matrices]] that are also [[Band matrix|band matrices]], meaning that their non-zero entries are confined to a diagonal ''band'', comprising the [[main diagonal]] and zero or more diagonals on each side.<ref name=":4">{{Citation |last=Bourgade |first=Paul |chapter=Random band matrices |date=2018-06-06 |title=Proceedings of the International Congress of Mathematicians (ICM 2018) |pages=2759–2783 |chapter-url=https://www.worldscientific.com/doi/abs/10.1142/9789813272880_0159 |access-date=2025-08-17 |publisher=WORLD SCIENTIFIC |doi=10.1142/9789813272880_0159 |isbn=978-981-327-287-3|arxiv=1807.03031 }}. [[arxiv:1807.03031|Available]] on ArXiv.</ref> They can be used to roughly model systems of interacting particles arranged roughly in a grid such that each particle is only allowed to interact with its neighbors, which is an improvement on the [[Mean-field theory|mean field model]], corresponding to random Gaussian matrices, where no entries are necessarily zero and every particle interacts with every other.<ref name=":4" />

In one dimension, this means that <math display="inline">H_{ij} = 0</math> if <math display="inline">|i - j| > W</math>, where W is the band width.<ref name=":4" /> Physically, this means that the amount by which particles ''i'' and ''j'' interact is 0 if their separation is over W.<ref name=":4" /> In more than one dimension, i and j are no longer integers but ''n''d vectors with integer components, and <math display="inline">H_{ij} = 0</math> if <math>|i - j|_{L^1}</math>, where <math>|\cdot|_{L^1}</math> indicates the [[taxicab distance]] between the two locations.<ref name=":4" />

== Anderson's model ==
Random band matrices are relevant to the study of [[Anderson localization|Anderson's model of electron localization]], which attempts to explain why metals with small amounts of impurities added hit a sudden transition where they cease to be conductive and start to insulate.<ref name=":0">{{Cite web |last=Sloman |first=Leila |date=2025-08-15 |title=New Physics-Inspired Proof Probes the Borders of Disorder |url=https://www.quantamagazine.org/new-physics-inspired-proof-probes-the-borders-of-disorder-20250815/ |access-date=2025-08-17 |website=Quanta Magazine |language=en}}</ref> The interaction potentials of certain particles ''i'', ''j'', in the model form a matrix; specifically a band matrix, as particles only interact with their neighbors.<ref name=":0" /> Anderson's matrices always have a thin band.<ref name=":0" /> However, as only some of the entries in Anderson's model are random, it is not a random band matrix.<ref name=":0" /> The study of random band matrices, however, is related.<ref name=":0" />
